column2: As Rama's messenger I say: give Sita to Raghava, or you will die, slain by Rama's arrows together with the Rakshasas in Lanka — certainly.
Ravana, eager to kill him, was restrained by Vibhishana; Maruti set his tail ablaze, with his tail on fire.
Having burned Lanka and the Rakshasas, seen Sita and bowed to her, he came across the sea and said, "Sita has been seen."
Angada and the others, drinking honey in Madhuvana and defeating Dadhimukha and others, saw Rama and said to him:
Sita has been seen. Rama too, delighted, asked Maruti: "How did you see Sita, and what did she say to me?
Sprinkle me with the nectar of the tale of Sita, I who am gone into the fire of longing." Hanuman said to Rama, having leapt across the ocean:
Having seen Sita and burned the city, take the jewel of Sita. Having slain Ravana you will obtain Sita, Rama; do not grieve.
Taking that jewel, Rama wept, afflicted with separation: "Seeing the jewel, Janaki is seen by me; take me to Sita.
Without her I cannot live." Comforted by Sugriva and others, he went to the sea shore; there Vibhishana came to Rama,
driven off by his brother, the evil-minded Ravana, who was told "Give Sita to Rama" — helpless.
Rama anointed his friend Vibhishana in the lordship of Lanka. When the ocean did not give a way though asked, then with arrows
he pierced it; the ocean came and said to Rama: "Bridging me with Nala, go to Lanka; I am deep.
I was made by you before." Rama too, by the bridge of Nala made with trees and rocks, crossed the great ocean with the monkeys; standing on Suvela he saw Lanka.
The abduction of Sita is a sin done by you, since you are my elder; therefore I go to fight, to slay Rama with the monkeys.
So saying, Kumbhakarna crushed all the monkeys; seizing Sugriva, he cut off his ears and nose.
Without ears and nose, Sugriva ate monkeys; then Rama cut off Kumbhakarna's arms with arrows,
then his feet, and cast his head to the ground. Then Kumbha, Nikumbha and the Rakshasa Makaraksha,
Mahodara, Mahaparshva, the Rakshasas Matta and Unmatta, Pragasa, Bhasakarna and Virupaksha in battle,
Devantaka, Narantaka, Trishiras and Atikaya — these were by Rama, Lakshmana, the monkeys and Vibhishana,
and other Rakshasas fighting were laid on the earth. Indrajit, fighting by magic, bound Rama and the others.
By serpent-arrows given as a boon, the two were freed of the arrows by an herb; made free of wounds by the herb brought by Maruti on the mountain,
Hanuman held the mountain where it stood. Lakshmana, seeing him performing oblations at Nikumbhila,
slew the hero Indrajit in battle with arrows. Ravana, burning with grief, rose to kill Sita,
restrained by Avindhya, the king went in his chariot with his army. Told by Indra, Matali had Rama mount the chariot.
The fight of Rama and Ravana was like that of Rama and Ravana. Ravana slew monkeys and Maruti and others slew Ravana.
Rama grew with weapons and missiles like a cloud. He cut down his banner, his chariot, horses and charioteer,
his bow, arms and heads; and heads rose up again. With the Paitamaha missile Rama split Ravana's heart.
Felled to the ground by all the Rakshasas, the women wept. Having consoled them and done his rites, Vibhishana, commanded by Rama,
brought Sita by Hanuman; Rama accepted Sita, pure, who had entered the fire, praised by Indra and others.
By Brahma and Dasharatha: "You are Vishnu, the destroyer of the Rakshasa." Worshipped by Indra, he revived the monkeys with a rain of nectar.
Honored by Rama, having seen the battle they went to heaven. Rama gave Lanka to Vibhishana, having honored the monkeys,
with Sita stood in the Pushpaka and went by the road he had come, showing Sita the forest fastnesses with joyful mind.
Saluting Bharadvaja he came to Nandigrama; bowed to by Bharata, he went to Ayodhya and stayed there.
Having saluted Vasishtha and others, Kaushalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra, having received the kingdom, he honored the Brahmins and the rest.
He then worshipped Vasudeva, his own Self, with horse-sacrifices. He gave all gifts and protected the people.

Like sons, devoted to dharma, desire and the rest and to punishing the wicked; the people were devoted to all dharma, the earth had abundant crops; there was no untimely death while Rama ruled the kingdom.
So saying, the Brahmins Agastya and others, saluted, went; Shatrughna, told by Rama and requested by the gods, slew Lavana.
A city, Mathura, came to be; told by Rama, Bharata slew three crores of the sons of Shailusha with sharp arrows,
Shailusha the wicked Gandharva dwelling on the Sindhu's bank; and having set Taksha and Pushkara his sons in the two countries,
Bharata went with Shatrughna and stayed honoring Raghava. Rama, having slain the wicked in battle and protected the good, the man,
two excellent sons Kusha and Lava were born in Valmiki's hermitage; she had been abandoned because of the people's slander, and they were recognized by hearing his good conduct.
Having anointed them in the kingdom, absorbed in the meditation "I am Brahman," for ten thousand years and ten hundred years
having ruled and performed sacrifices, he went to heaven honored by the gods, with the citizens, with his brothers, with Sita's sons and the people of the country.
Agni said: Valmiki, having heard from Narada, composed the Ramayana; whoever hears it in detail goes to heaven.
Kamsa too sent Putana and others to destroy the child; they were entrusted by Vasudeva to Nanda, husband of Yashoda,
for protection from Kamsa and others, out of fear, in Gokula. Rama and Krishna roamed there with cows and cowherds.
The two became the cowherd protectors of the whole world. Krishna was bound to a mortar with a rope by the distracted Yashoda;
he went between the twin arjuna trees, and the twin arjuna trees were broken; a cart was overturned by a kick of the one seeking the breast.
Putana, who was ready to kill, was slain by his drinking at her breast. Krishna went to Vrindavana; Kaliya from the pool of the Yamuna
he conquered, drove out and placed in the ocean, praised by Balarama. He made the Talavana safe, killing the ass Dhenuka,
killed the bull Arishta and Keshin in the form of a horse; having abandoned the festival of Indra, he had the Govardhana sacrifice made.
Having held up the mountain, the rain from Indra was warded off; Govinda, bowed to by Mahendra, was then presented to Arjuna.
The festival of Indra was again made by Krishna, pleased. Riding a chariot he went to Mathura, praised by Akrura sent by Kamsa.
He was looked upon by the gopis, devoted and sporting; he slew the washerman who did not give him garments and took the clothes.
With Rama he gave a boon to the garland-maker who offered garlands; he made the hunchback, who gave ointment, straight; he killed the elephant
Kuvalayapida, maddened, at the gate, entered the arena, and while Kamsa and others on the platforms watched, a wrestling bout
was done with Chanura the wrestler; Bala fought Mushtika. Chanura and Mushtika were slain by them, and other wrestlers too.
Having slain Kamsa, lord of Mathura, and his father, Hari made the Yadava king; and Kamsa's wives Asti and Prapti
were daughters of Jarasandha; Jarasandha, urged by them, besieged Mathura and fought the Yadavas with arrows.
Rama and Krishna left Mathura and came to Gomanta. Having conquered Jarasandha in battle, and Paundraka Vasudeva,
and having made the city of Dvaraka, he dwelt surrounded by Yadavas. Having slain Bhauma Naraka, the maidens brought by him
of gods, Gandharvas and Yakshas — Janardana spoke to them: sixteen thousand women, and eight Rukmini and others.
With Satyabhama on Garuda, the slayer of Naraka took the jewel mountain and, having conquered Indra in heaven, Hari
brought the Parijata and set it in Satyabhama's house. Having learned weapons and missiles from Sandipani, he gave back his son.
Having conquered the demon Panchajana, honored by Yama, he killed Kalayavana, honored by Muchukunda.
He worshipped Vasudeva and Devaki and devoted Brahmins. Of Revati and Balabhadra were born Nishatha and Ulmuka.
From Krishna and Jambavati was born Samba; of the other wives, other sons.
Shambara gave that fish to Mayavati.
Mayavati, seeing in the fish her husband, lovingly nourished him and said: "I am your Rati; you are my husband.
You are Kama, made bodiless by Shambhu; I was made so by Shambara. You were not taken by him as wife; knowing magic, slay Shambara."
Hearing that, Pradyumna, having slain Shambara, went with his wife Mayavati to Krishna; Krishna and Rukmini were delighted.
From Pradyumna was born Aniruddha, husband of Usha, of noble mind; Bana, son of Bali, had a daughter Usha and the city of Shonita.
By austerity he became Shiva's son, felled by the peacock-bannered one; Shiva, pleased, said to Bana: "You will obtain battle, Bana."
Seeing Gauri sporting with Shiva, Usha longed for a husband. Gauri said to her: "Your husband will be seen sleeping at night.
On the twelfth day of the month of Vaisakha, a man will be your husband." Told by Gauri, delighted, Usha slept in her house and saw him.
Knowing she was united with him, her friend Chitralekha brought Aniruddha from a drawn picture,
Krishna's grandson, from Dvaraka — the daughter of Bana's minister Kumbhanda. Aniruddha went and sported with Usha.
By the falling of Bana's banner he was reported by the guards. A terrible fight occurred between Aniruddha and Bana.
Hearing from Narada, Krishna with Pradyumna and Balabhadra, on Garuda, then conquered the fires and the fever of Maheshvara.
Then occurred a fight between Hari and Shankara, arrow against arrow; Nandi, Vinayaka, Skanda and the leaders were conquered by Tarkshya and the others.
When Shankara yawned and was undone by Vishnu with the yawning missile, a thousand arms were cut; Rudra begged for fearlessness.
Revived by Vishnu, Bana, two-armed, said to Shiva: "The fearlessness given by you to this Bana, I too give.
There is no difference between us two; he who differentiates goes to hell." Vishnu, worshipped by Shiva and others, with Aniruddha and Usha,
went to Dvaraka and delighted with Ugrasena and the Yadavas. Aniruddha's son was Vajra, who from Markandeya became all-knowing.
Balabhadra, slayer of Pralamba, became the one who drew the Yamuna, breaker of the monkey Dvivida, destroyer of the Kaurava madness.
Hari, the Lord of many forms, sported with Rukmini and others and begot countless Yadava sons. Whoever recites the Harivamsha, having his wishes fulfilled, goes to Hari.
Karna, born of the maiden Kunti, depended on Duryodhana; by fate enmity arose between the Kurus and the Pandavas.
The evil-minded Duryodhana burned the Pandavas in the house of lac; the Pandavas, led by their mother, came out of the burnt house.
Then at Ekachakra, in a Brahmin's dwelling, all stayed in sages' dress after slaying the demon Baka.
They went to the country of Panchala for Draupadi's svayamvara; by piercing the target Draupadi was won by the five Pandavas.
Then they received half the kingdom, being recognized by Duryodhana and others; the divine bow Gandiva and the best chariot from Agni,
and Arjuna had Krishna as charioteer in battle, and inexhaustible arrows; and from Drona the Brahma weapon and others; all were skilled in weapons.
With Krishna, Arjuna satisfied Agni at Khandava; the Pandava, warding off Indra's rain with a shower of arrows.
The directions were conquered by the Pandavas and Yudhishthira ruled; the Rajasuya with much gold Suyodhana could not bear.
Told by his brother Duhshasana and by Karna, who had gained power, in a game of dice by Shakuni,
he won from Yudhishthira by dice his kingdom as well; seated in the hall he laughed by illusion. Defeated, Yudhishthira with his brothers went to the forest.
In the forest he passed the twelve years as vowed, feeding eighty-eight thousand Brahmins as before.
With Dhaumya and Draupadi as the sixth, he then went to Virata: Kanka the Brahmin, unknown, the king; Bhima the cook,
Arjuna Brihannala, the wife Sairandhri, and the twins; under another name Bhimasena slew Kichaka in the night.
Arjuna conquered the Kurus when they wished to seize Draupadi; during their cattle raid and other acts the Pandavas were then recognized by them.
Subhadra, Krishna's sister, bore Abhimanyu from Arjuna; Virata gave him his daughter Uttara.
The king Dharmaraja became lord of seven akshauhinis for battle; Krishna as envoy went and spoke to the intolerant Duryodhana,
the king lord of eleven akshauhinis, then: "Give Yudhishthira half the kingdom, or five villages,
or fight." Hearing the words, Suyodhana said to Krishna: "I will not give even a needle-point of land; I shall fight, ready for battle."
Having shown the universal form, invincible, honored by Vidura, he went back and said to Yudhishthira: "Fight this Suyodhana."
Shikhandi was of the Pandavas, and a fight occurred between them. The Dhartarashtras with Bhishma struck the Pandavas in battle.
Shikhandi and the other Pandavas struck the Dhartarashtras in the fight; a war like that of gods and demons between the armies of the Kurus and Pandavas
occurred, increasing the joy of the gods in heaven who watched. Bhishma with missiles felled the Pandava army for ten days.
On the tenth day Arjuna rained arrows on the hero Bhishma; Shikhandi, told by Drupada, rained missiles like a cloud.
Elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers were felled by each other's missiles; Bhishma, whose death was by his own will, showed the way of battle.
